name: Darwin's finches: the birds he misfiled
scope: The most famous story in biology, told with the honest chronology — and then handed to the people who actually measured it. T1: HMS Beagle was at sea five years (27 Dec 1831 – 2 Oct 1836), but Darwin was in the Galapagos for only five weeks (15 Sept – 20 Oct 1835) and set foot on just four islands. T2: he did NOT have the finch insight aboard — he filed the birds as wrens, blackbirds and grosbeaks, and mostly failed to record which island each came from. T3: back in London the ornithologist John Gould examined the skins and reported to the Zoological Society in January 1837 that they were not a mixed bag at all but one closely allied group of ground finches, several confined to single islands — THAT is when it landed, from someone else's expertise. T4: to rescue the island data Darwin had to beg specimens off shipmates who HAD labelled theirs — Captain FitzRoy, FitzRoy's steward Harry Fuller, and Darwin's own servant Syms Covington. T5: the birds that actually moved him at the time were the MOCKINGBIRDS, which he had labelled island by island, and whose differences prompted his 1835 notebook remark that such facts would undermine the stability of species. T6: 'Darwin's finches' is not Darwin's phrase — Percy Lowe coined it in 1936 and David Lack's 1947 book made it famous; the Origin never singles them out. T7: they are not finches — DNA places all 18 species in Thraupidae, the TANAGER family, descended from one South American grassquit-like colonist that arrived 1–2 million years ago. T8: Peter and Rosemary Grant went to Daphne Major in 1973 and began banding and measuring every bird on the island, year after year. T9: the 1977 drought killed roughly 84% of the medium ground finches; only the big tough Tribulus seeds were left, and the survivors had measurably deeper beaks — selection measured in ONE generation. T10: the 1983 El Nino deluge flooded the island with small soft seeds and swung selection back the other way — the beaks OSCILLATE, which is what real selection looks like. T11: the 'Big Bird' lineage — a single immigrant male arriving in 1981 founded a line that became reproductively isolated by song and beak size within a few generations. T12: the woodpecker finch uses a cactus spine as a tool, and the sharp-beaked ground finch on Wolf and Darwin islands drinks the blood of nesting boobies. T13: honest caveat — 40 years of data show selection acting hard and repeatedly, but not marching in a single direction; the Grants' record is evidence of the MECHANISM working, not of a straight line to somewhere.
source: Grokipedia, 'Darwin's finches' (Beagle dates, Galapagos 15 Sept–20 Oct 1835, four islands, 31 specimens/9 species, Darwin's misidentifications as wrens/blackbirds/grosbeaks, Covington, Gould 1837, Thraupidae/Geospizinae, 18 species, 1977 drought ~4% body-size shift, Big Bird lineage from 1981); Wikipedia, 'Darwin's finches' (Percy Lowe 1936 coinage, David Lack 1947, Gould's 10 Jan 1837 Zoological Society report, FitzRoy and Harry Fuller as labelled-specimen sources, mockingbirds vs finches in Darwin's own attention, Origin does not single out the finches); Boag & Grant 1981 (Science) and Grant & Grant, '40 Years of Evolution' (2014) flagged for numeric verification at build time.
framing_note: DISCOVERY + CORRECTED-MISCONCEPTION keystone. T1 keys the SCALE MISMATCH (five years at sea, five weeks in the islands) — never a bare date. ACCURACY RAILS: (a) Gould reported to the Zoological Society on 10 January 1837 and sources differ on whether he said 12 or 13 species — key the rung on WHO told Darwin and WHAT he said (one closely allied group, not unrelated wrens and blackbirds), never on the count; (b) NEVER claim Darwin had the idea while standing in the Galapagos — the insight arrived in London, months later, from another man's expertise, and this correction is the ladder's spine; (c) the Grant figures (~84% mortality, ~4–5% morphological shift) must be checked against Boag & Grant 1981 before authoring — approximate is fine, invented is not. DINNER-TEST PAYOFF: the mockingbird rung and the 'they aren't finches, they're tanagers' rung. DISTRACTOR MINE: real naturalists who genuinely handled parts of the Beagle collection (Richard Owen on the fossil mammals, Thomas Bell on the reptiles, Leonard Jenyns on the fish) so all four choices stay live; plus the real wrong groups Darwin himself wrote on the labels. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let a stem say 'one ancestral species diversified into many' before asking what Gould told him — describe the crate of skins and the confusion, and let the knowledge be recalled. LANE: the animal bank owns beak biomechanics as a creature adaptation; this ladder owns how we KNOW and how the story got mistold.
history_overlap: geography bank may run a Galapagos/Ecuador place ladder (volcanic archipelago, Humboldt Current) — this ladder must not tour the islands; animal bank may own finch tool-use and the vampire finch as creature marvels (T12 here is a one-line evidence rung, not a portrait) — check before authoring; history bank Victorian Britain / the Beagle as a survey voyage.

name: Twenty years of silence and Wallace's envelope
scope: Why the most important book in biology was nearly never written, and what forced it. T1: Darwin had the mechanism worked out by 1838 and published in 1859 — he sat on it for over twenty years, and spent eight of them on barnacles instead. T2: in 1842 he wrote a pencil sketch, and by July 1844 a 230-page essay, which he left in a drawer with a letter to Emma asking her to have it published if he died suddenly. T3: on 18 June 1858 a letter reached Down House from Alfred Russel Wallace, collecting specimens in the Malay Archipelago, enclosing an essay that laid out essentially the same mechanism; Darwin wrote to Lyell that his originality would be 'smashed'. T4: Charles Lyell and Joseph Hooker arranged a joint reading at the Linnean Society on 1 July 1858 — without asking Wallace, who was still in the East Indies and learned of it afterwards. T5: Darwin was not there either. His infant son Charles Waring had died of scarlet fever on 28 June, and Darwin was at the funeral while his life's work was read aloud. T6: the reading landed with a thud — the Linnean Society's president Thomas Bell reported that the year 1858 had 'not, indeed, been marked by any of those striking discoveries which at once revolutionize' science. T7: the shock made Darwin write fast; On the Origin of Species appeared on 24 November 1859 in a print run of 1,250, and the trade took essentially all of it on the first day, with Mudie's circulating library alone taking 500. T8: Wallace's own conduct is the surprise of the story — he named the theory 'Darwinism', dedicated his 1869 book The Malay Archipelago to Darwin, and never claimed he had been robbed. T9: what Darwin still could not explain was HEREDITY — his own proposal, pangenesis, was wrong, and the answer was already in print (Mendel, 1866) and unread for decades. T10: the caveat historians actually argue about — why he waited. Illness, the size of the project, Emma's faith, the fate of the anonymous author of Vestiges (1844): the reason is disputed, and the bank says so.
source: Wikipedia, 'On the Origin of Species' (18 June 1858 receipt of Wallace's essay, Darwin's 'smashed' letter to Lyell, 1 July 1858 joint reading, 24 Nov 1859 publication, 1,250 print run, ~1,170 for sale, 500 to Mudie's, the 1842 sketch and 230-page 1844 Essay); Wikipedia, 'Publication of Darwin's theory' (Charles Waring Darwin's scarlet fever 23 June, death 28 June, funeral on 1 July concurrent with the reading; Thomas Bell's verbatim presidential remark; Lyell and Hooker arranged the reading; Wallace not consulted, responded January 1859); Darwin Correspondence Project (letter to Emma Darwin, 5 July 1844) flagged for verification of the publication bequest.
framing_note: DISCOVERY ladder about priority, nerve and grief. T1 keys the DELAY — a number so odd it demands an explanation — never a date-recall stem. ACCURACY RAILS: (a) Darwin's 1844 instruction to Emma is real but the sum he set aside (commonly quoted as £400) must be verified in the Darwin Correspondence Project letter of 5 July 1844 before it becomes a rung; if it cannot be sourced, key the rung on the instruction, not the amount; (b) NEVER say Wallace 'agreed to' the joint reading — he was not asked, and the honest version is better; (c) do not assert 'he delayed because he feared the Church' as settled fact — historians dispute it, so the T10 rung frames it AS disputed or the rung is dropped. DINNER-TEST PAYOFF: T5 — a man at his baby son's funeral while his twenty-year secret is read to a half-empty room. DISTRACTOR MINE: real contemporaries and real rival mechanisms — Lamarck's use-inheritance, Robert Chambers' anonymous Vestiges of the Natural History of Creation (1844), Lyell's uniformitarianism, Richard Owen's archetypes, Wallace's own later spiritualism. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: the stem supplies the SCENE (an envelope from the Malay islands, a panicked letter to Lyell) and never states the mechanism the answer names.
history_overlap: history bank may own Victorian Britain and the social reception of Darwinism (the 1860 Huxley–Wilberforce exchange in particular) — this ladder stops at publication and does not stage the debate; philosophy bank owns Paley's design argument and the is/ought misuse of 'Darwinism'; any Mendel ladder in the heredity sub-strand owns Mendel — the T9 rung here is only Darwin's missing piece.

name: Natural selection: an algorithm with no foresight
scope: CONCEPT ladder — the mechanism itself, deepened across the named cases that display it. T1: Darwin's book opens not with wild animals but with PIGEONS — fantails, pouters, tumblers, all descended from one rock dove, because he wanted his reader to SEE what selection does inside a single human lifetime before asking them to believe it over millions. T2: the recipe has exactly three ingredients — more offspring are born than can survive, they vary, and the variation is inherited. That is the whole engine, and nothing in it requires anyone to intend anything. T3: the third ingredient came from an economist — Darwin read Thomas Malthus on population in September 1838 and saw at once that a struggle for existence was arithmetically unavoidable. T4: selection has no foresight and cannot start over. The recurrent laryngeal nerve leaves the brain, runs PAST the larynx, all the way down the neck, loops under the aorta, and comes back up — in a giraffe that detour runs several metres for a journey of centimetres. That is not a design; it is an inherited plan being edited. T5: 'survival of the fittest' is not Darwin's phrase — Herbert Spencer coined it, and Darwin only adopted it in the fifth edition of the Origin (1869), at Wallace's urging; 'fittest' means best-FITTING the local situation, not strongest or best. T6: selection is not the only thing that happens — teach genetic DRIFT before testing it: in small populations, traits can spread by sheer sampling luck, with no advantage at all. T7: an anti-anthropomorphism rung — populations evolve; individuals do not. Nothing tries to adapt, and no giraffe ever needed anything. T8: Darwin invented a SECOND mechanism because the first could not explain a peacock — sexual selection, published in 1871, exists precisely because a tail that huge is a survival liability. T9: what the theory FORBIDS is what makes it testable — nothing in the theory permits a mammal in Precambrian rock, and no one has ever found one. T10: the strongest objection Darwin faced in his lifetime was not religious but engineering — Fleeming Jenkin argued in 1867 that under blending inheritance any new advantage would be diluted away in a few generations; Darwin had no answer, and particulate inheritance was the answer he never saw.
source: Wikipedia, 'Natural selection' (Malthus 1838 and the 'favourable variations would tend to be preserved' formulation; artificial selection and pigeon fanciers as Darwin's opening analogy; Spencer's coinage and Darwin's fifth-edition (1869) adoption with Darwin's own quoted concession; the three conditions — variation, heritability, differential reproduction); Grokipedia, 'Vestigiality' (Darwin, Origin ch.13, on rudimentary and aborted organs; developmental constraint as the reason reduction is incomplete); Darwin, On the Origin of Species ch.1 and Darwin Correspondence Project flagged for verification of his personal pigeon breeding and club memberships; Fleeming Jenkin's 1867 North British Review critique.
framing_note: The ANALYTIC BACKBONE of the sub-strand — a concept ladder built entirely from named cases, carrying native T4/T5 ceiling. ACCURACY RAILS: (a) verify from the Darwin Correspondence Project and Origin ch.1 that Darwin personally kept and bred pigeons and joined London pigeon clubs before keying T1 on it — if only the analogy is documented, key the rung on the ARGUMENT (he made his reader watch selection happen first) not the hobby; (b) the giraffe recurrent-laryngeal figure must be checked before a number is used — key the rung on the ROUTE, which is unambiguous, rather than the metres; (c) the 'no rabbits in the Precambrian' line attributed to Haldane is a widely repeated anecdote with contested provenance — T9 must state the falsification test in the bank's own words rather than quote an unsourced Haldane; (d) NEVER anthropomorphize: no 'evolution wants', 'nature selects for', 'the species needed'. VISION_MANDATED TRUE: evolution by natural selection sits in the bank's FIRM + CELEBRATED list, so the moral audit must check BOTH failure directions on this ladder — no false balance smuggled in from design arguments, AND no sermonizing at religion. The honest line is that the mechanism needs no designer in order to work, stated flatly as science, with nothing said about what that does or does not imply. DINNER-TEST PAYOFF: T4, the nerve that goes the wrong way. DISTRACTOR MINE: the real graveyard of respectable-but-wrong evolutionary theories — Lamarckian use-inheritance, orthogenesis, saltationism, Darwin's own pangenesis, blending inheritance — each of which serious biologists genuinely held.
history_overlap: philosophy bank owns Paley's watchmaker as a reasoning move and the is/ought fallacy behind 'social Darwinism' — this ladder stays on the mechanism and never argues design; science's own eugenics/dark-chapters ladder (howscience section) owns the political misuse of selection; animal bank owns any specific creature's adaptation, including the peacock's tail as a display — T8 here keys why Darwin needed a SECOND mechanism, not the bird.

name: Tiktaalik: they knew where to dig
scope: Evolution as a theory that tells you where to point the shovel — and the honest correction that followed. T1: Neil Shubin's team did not stumble on Tiktaalik. They decided in advance what they needed — a fish with a neck and a wrist — worked out what age of rock could hold it, and then went looking for rock of that age. T2: the arithmetic that set the target: lobe-finned fish are abundant by about 385 million years ago and true four-limbed animals appear by about 365, so the intermediate had to lie between; the rock also had to be freshwater sediment, and exposed at the surface. A geology map pointed to the Devonian Fram Formation on Ellesmere Island, Nunavut, more than 700 miles north of the Arctic Circle. T3: it did not work quickly — expeditions from 1999 onward found nothing that mattered, until the 2004 field season, when a flat snout appeared in the cliff face. T4: what the rock gave up, from about 375 million years ago: a flat crocodile-shaped skull with the eyes on TOP, spiracles behind them, and — decisively — a NECK, because the shoulder girdle had come loose from the skull. No fish can turn its head. T5: inside the fin was a humerus, a radius and an ulna, and small wrist bones, with an elbow that could bend about ninety degrees — a fin that could do a push-up — still tipped with lepidotrichia, ordinary fish fin-rays. Not a limb: a fin with a limb inside it. T6: the name came from Inuit elders in Nunavut, from their word for a large fish of shallow fresh water — the naming was asked for, not imposed. T7: the honest caveat, and the best rung on the ladder — in 2010 fossil TRACKWAYS turned up in a quarry at Zachelmie in Poland, dated to roughly 395 million years ago, about 18 million years OLDER than Tiktaalik. Something with feet was already walking before Tiktaalik lived. The prediction still worked; the word 'ancestor' did not. T8: a further twist from the same Arctic rocks — Qikiqtania wakei, described in 2022, is a close relative whose arm bone went BACK toward paddling. The group was experimenting in both directions, not marching toward land. T9: a 2024 micro-CT scan of the original skull-and-skeleton specimen revealed 25 trunk vertebrae with broad ribs and gastralia — belly ribs — the equipment for holding your own weight up out of water.
source: Grokipedia, 'Tiktaalik' (Shubin, Daeschler and Farish Jenkins; surveys from 1999 and the 2004 field season; Fram Formation, Ellesmere Island, Nunavut, late Frasnian ~375 Mya; NUFV 108 holotype; the two companion Nature papers of 2006; detached pectoral girdle and mobile neck, dorsal eyes, spiracles, humerus/radius/ulna plus radials with retained lepidotrichia, ~90-degree elbow flexion; Inuktitut naming via consultation with Inuit elders; the 2010 Zachelmie quarry trackways at ~395 Mya predating Tiktaalik by ~18 Myr; Qikiqtania wakei 2022; the 2024 micro-CT axial-skeleton study, 25 trunk vertebrae, gastralia); Daeschler, Shubin & Jenkins, Nature 440 (2006).
framing_note: The flagship 'evolution makes testable predictions' ladder — the payoff is that a theory told a team WHERE and WHEN to dig and the rock delivered. ACCURACY RAILS: (a) do NOT call Tiktaalik 'our ancestor' — the 2010 Zachelmie trackways make it a late-surviving member of the transitional group, and teaching that correction IS the ladder's most on-voice moment, not a blemish to hide; (b) the name is glossed 'large freshwater fish' in the original Nature paper and 'large shallow-water fish' elsewhere — key the rung on WHO named it (Nunavut Inuit elders were asked) rather than on the exact gloss; (c) sources differ on the month of the 2004 find — say 'the 2004 field season', not a month. DINNER-TEST PAYOFF: T1/T2 — they predicted the age of the rock and went there. DISTRACTOR MINE: real adjacent fossils and real rival candidates, all of which serious paleontologists have placed near this transition — Panderichthys, Eusthenopteron, Elpistostege, Acanthostega, Ichthyostega, plus the living coelacanth and lungfish. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never put 'a fish with a wrist' in the stem and then ask what they found — describe the SEARCH (the age arithmetic, the Arctic map, the empty summers) and let the animal be recalled knowledge.
history_overlap: geography bank may own Ellesmere Island / the Canadian High Arctic as a place — this ladder keeps the Arctic as the setting of a prediction, never a tour; animal bank owns the coelacanth, lungfish and mudskipper as living creatures — they appear here only as distractors.

name: Lenski's twelve flasks
scope: Evolution running live, in a rack of flasks, since before most parents were born. T1: on 24 February 1988 Richard Lenski put twelve identical flasks of E. coli on a shaker — and they have been fed by hand every single day since, past 80,000 generations. T2: the food is deliberately meagre: a minimal medium with 25 micrograms of glucose per millilitre, so every population starves every afternoon; each morning 1% of each flask is moved into fresh medium, about six or seven doublings a day. T3: the thing that makes it an experiment rather than a very long culture — every 500 generations a sample is frozen at minus eighty. The ancestors are ALIVE in a freezer, and any descendant can be thawed out and raced directly against its own great-great-grandparent in the same flask. T4: those races are the measurement — fitness is read off a competition, not guessed. The populations were about 37% fitter than the ancestor by generation 2,000 and roughly 70% fitter by 50,000, and the curve has still not gone flat; it only climbs more slowly. T5: because there are twelve, you can watch the tape run twelve times. Every one of them independently evolved larger cells — parallel evolution, seen not once but a dozen times over. T6: around generation 31,500 one population, labelled Ara-3, did the thing E. coli is textbook-defined as unable to do: eat citrate in the presence of oxygen. The citrate had been sitting in the medium the entire time — an untouched meal at the bottom of the flask for thirty-one thousand generations. T7: the best rung, and the reason the freezer exists — they could test whether it was a fluke by replaying it. Restarting from LATE frozen ancestors produced the innovation again; restarting from early ones did not. Earlier mutations had to be in place first: the door had to be unlocked before it could be opened. T8: several populations broke their own DNA-repair genes and became hypermutators — mutating faster paid off at first and cost them later, as harmful mutations piled up. T9: honest caveat — it did not start in Michigan. It began at UC Irvine in 1988, moved to Michigan State in 1990 and to UT Austin in 2022 before returning; and it survives entirely on someone showing up every day, which is the least glamorous and most necessary fact about it.
source: Grokipedia, 'E. coli long-term evolution experiment' (start 24 Feb 1988 at UC Irvine; move to Michigan State 1990, UT Austin 2022, return; Jeffrey Barrick; 12 populations from REL606/REL607 with the neutral Ara marker; DM25 with 25 ug/mL glucose plus unusable citrate; daily 1:100 transfer, ~6.6 generations/day; freezing every 500 generations at -80C in 15% glycerol and the revival protocol; >80,000 generations as of Nov 2025; Malthusian-parameter competition assays; ~37% fitness gain by generation 2,000 and ~70% by 50,000 with continuing but diminishing gains; parallel increase in cell size across all twelve; Cit+ in population Ara-3 around generation 31,500 with gene amplification and promoter capture; replay experiments confirming potentiation and historical contingency; hypermutator lineages via mutS/mutL defects).
framing_note: The 'evolution is not a story about the past — it is happening in a flask this afternoon' ladder. T1 keys the ABSURD CONTINUITY (fed by hand, every day, for nearly forty years). ACCURACY RAILS: (a) it began at UC Irvine and moved to Michigan State in 1990 — say it right; the common retelling 'a Michigan lab since 1988' is wrong and correcting it is on-voice; (b) the generation count rises constantly — write the rung so it cannot go stale ('past 75,000') and verify the current figure at authoring time; (c) Cit+ arose in population Ara-3 around generation 31,500 — approximate is fine, precise is better, invented is forbidden. DINNER-TEST PAYOFF: T6, the meal that sat in the flask untouched for 31,500 generations, and T3, ancestors alive in a freezer. DISTRACTOR MINE: real adjacent microbiology, all of which a working scientist would have to rule out — contamination, horizontal gene transfer, plasmid uptake, phage — plus the real historical wrong answers: spontaneous generation, and directed/Lamarckian mutation, which the genuine Luria–Delbrick fluctuation test (on the same E. coli B lineage) killed in 1943. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never write 'a frozen fossil record' into a stem and then ask what makes the replay experiments possible.
history_overlap: science's own 'how science works' sub-strand may own replication and self-correction as a method idea — keep the freezer-and-replay rungs here as this experiment's specific machinery, and leave the general argument there; any Luria–Delbrick ladder in the microbiology sub-strand owns the fluctuation test itself (used here only as a distractor).

name: Resistance: evolution you can watch in a hospital
scope: CONCEPT ladder — natural selection observed in the one place everybody eventually visits. T1: the man who discovered penicillin predicted its failure. In his 1945 Nobel lecture Alexander Fleming warned that once the drug could be bought in shops, 'the ignorant man may easily underdose himself and by exposing his microbes to non-lethal quantities of the drug make them resistant'. T2: in 2016 Michael Baym and Roy Kishony made it visible — a huge agar plate divided into bands of steadily rising antibiotic concentration, with E. coli released at the edges and filmed on time-lapse conquering band after band in a matter of days, each new advance a visible fan spreading out of a single mutant. T3: the mechanisms are concrete and different from one another — enzymes that chop the drug apart (beta-lactamases cutting penicillin's ring), pumps that throw it back out of the cell (efflux pumps), and changed locks (MRSA's altered penicillin-binding protein). T4: bacteria do not always have to evolve resistance — they can be handed it. Plasmids ferry resistance genes between cells and even across species, so a harmless gut bacterium can arm a dangerous one. T5: the rung that reframes everything — resistance is not a modern invention. D'Costa and colleagues recovered beta-lactam, tetracycline and vancomycin resistance genes from 30,000-year-old Beringian permafrost, and bacteria taken from Lechuguilla Cave, sealed off from the surface for millions of years and never near a pharmacy, resist many modern drugs. Antibiotics are ancient chemical warfare between microbes; we did not start this war, we joined it. T6: what to actually do — 'always finish the course' is itself under test: a 2017 BMJ paper by Martin Llewelyn and colleagues argued the evidence for it is weak and that shorter courses are often as effective. The honest rung: take what your doctor prescribed, and notice that even the advice is being checked. T7: the arms race has a scoreboard — vancomycin was the last resort against MRSA until fully vancomycin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus was reported in 2002. T8: the pressure is not only medical — routine antibiotic use in livestock feed applies the same selection on a continental scale, which is why the EU banned growth-promoter use in 2006.
source: Wikipedia, 'Alexander Fleming' (the verbatim 1945 Nobel-lecture warning about the ignorant man underdosing himself, and his 26 June 1945 remark on 'penicillin-fast organisms'); Wikipedia, 'Antimicrobial resistance' (beta-lactamase inactivation, PBP target modification in MRSA, efflux pumps, reduced permeability, horizontal transfer of resistance genes via mobile elements); Baym et al., 'Spatiotemporal microbial evolution on antibiotic landscapes', Science 353 (2016) — flagged for verification of plate dimensions, concentration multiple and elapsed days; D'Costa et al., 'Antibiotic resistance is ancient', Nature 477 (2011) and Bhullar et al. on Lechuguilla Cave isolates (2012) — flagged for verification; Llewelyn et al., BMJ 358 (2017) on the 'finish the course' guidance.
framing_note: The sub-strand's 'this is happening to you, today' ladder. T1 keys FLEMING'S OWN WARNING and uses the documented Nobel-lecture wording verbatim — a real quote, cited, never paraphrased into something he did not say. ACCURACY RAILS: (a) every number in the MEGA-plate rung — plate size, the multiple of the lethal dose, the elapsed days — must be checked against Baym et al., Science 2016 before authoring; seed it, do not guess it, and if a figure cannot be confirmed, key the rung on the VISIBLE FANS spreading from single mutants, which is the paper's indisputable image; (b) the same discipline applies to D'Costa 2011 and the Lechuguilla isolates; (c) on 'finish the course', the bank PRESENTS the guidance and the live dispute and never issues medical instruction in its own voice — the safe and true line is 'take what you were prescribed'. DINNER-TEST PAYOFF: T5, resistance genes older than pharmacies by thirty thousand years. DISTRACTOR MINE: the genuinely common misconceptions, which are exactly the right wrong answers — that the PATIENT becomes resistant rather than the bacteria, that bacteria 'get used to' a drug the way a body builds tolerance, and Lamarckian directed adaptation; plus the real rival mechanisms (enzyme vs pump vs changed target). LANE BORDER: the DISCOVERY of penicillin — the 1928 contaminated dish, Florey and Chain, the wartime scale-up — belongs to the medicine/discovery sub-strand; this ladder may quote Fleming's 1945 warning but must NOT retell the discovery.
history_overlap: science's own penicillin-discovery ladder owns Fleming's 1928 dish and the Florey–Chain scale-up — this ladder keys only the 1945 resistance warning; history bank may own wartime penicillin production as a WWII story; any hospital-hygiene/Semmelweis ladder owns handwashing.

name: The whales that walked
scope: The best-documented big transition in the fossil record, and the moment two independent methods were forced to agree. T1: in 1834 Richard Harlan named an enormous fossil from the American South Basilosaurus — 'king lizard' — because he took it for a sea reptile. It was a whale, and by the rules of naming, the wrong name is stuck to it forever. T2: Richard Owen caught the error by looking at the TEETH: the molars had two roots, which no fish or reptile has. He proposed Zeuglodon, 'yoke tooth', and lost — the older name had priority. T3: 1983, Philip Gingerich, in Pakistan: Pakicetus, a wolf-sized land animal about 50 million years old, identified as a whale by its EAR — the skull carried the involucrum, a thickened bony lip on the ear bone found in whales and in nothing else alive or dead. T4: 1994, Hans Thewissen: Ambulocetus natans, 'the walking swimming whale' — about three metres long, crocodile-shaped, huge paddle-like hind feet, eyes set high, an ambush hunter in shallow water. T5: the legs shrink as you go up the rock column, and Wadi Al-Hitan in Egypt — Whale Valley — holds hundreds of skeletons that show it. Gingerich, Smith and Simons reported in 1990 a sixteen-metre Basilosaurus with complete hind limbs 35 centimetres long, with knee, ankle and toes: legs it could not possibly have walked on. T6: and those legs were probably not idle — the best current reading is that they served as claspers during mating. Vestigial means 'has lost its ancestral job', not 'does nothing'. T7: the payoff rung — molecular biologists said whales' closest living relatives were even-toed hoofed mammals, with hippos nearest; fossil specialists backed mesonychids, an extinct group of hoofed carnivores. In 2001 an ankle bone settled it: Pakicetus and Rodhocetus turned out to have the double-pulley astragalus, an ankle unique to artiodactyls. The molecules had been right, and the bones came round. T8: 2007, Indohyus — a raccoon-sized, deer-like raoellid from Kashmir, about 48 million years old, with limb bones thickened for wading and an ear bulla built like a whale's: a land animal already using the water. T9: the nostrils travel — across the sequence the nasal opening migrates from the tip of the snout back over the top of the skull, and becomes the blowhole. T10: an honest caveat about the record itself — the earliest members come from river red-beds that shift and shred fossils, the later ones from calm marine deposits that preserve hundreds of near-complete skeletons. The unevenness is about where mud settles, not about missing evidence.
source: Grokipedia, 'Evolution of cetaceans' (artiodactyl origin ~53.5 Mya; Indohyus as raoellid sister group, Kashmir, ~48 Mya, pachyosteosclerotic bones and thickened auditory bulla, 2007 phylogenetics and 2009 postcranial follow-up; Pakicetidae ~50 Mya northern Pakistan, dense limb bones as ballast, 2001 postcrania; Ambulocetus natans, Thewissen 1994, Kuldana Formation, ~3 m; Remingtonocetidae; Basilosauridae ~41–34 Mya as first obligately aquatic; the double-trochleated astragalus as artiodactyl synapomorphy documented in Pakicetus and Rodhocetus; Wadi Al-Hitan preservation bias — fluvial red-beds vs calm marine lagerstatten, 500+ Dorudon specimens); Wikipedia, 'Basilosaurus' (Harlan 1834 'king lizard' misidentified as marine reptile, Owen's two-rooted molars and proposed Zeuglodon cetoides, nomenclature priority; Gingerich, Smith & Simons 1990 at Wadi El Hitan — 35 cm hind limbs on a 16 m individual, fused tarsals, three digits, non-locomotory and probable mating claspers; B. cetoides 17–20 m).
framing_note: The canonical transitional SERIES — this sub-strand's answer to 'show me a fossil with legs turning into flippers'. T1 inverts the wonder: the hook is a whale that will be called 'king lizard' for all time, and the knowable thing is what it actually was. ACCURACY RAILS: (a) do NOT present the series as a straight ancestor-to-descendant chain — these are known members of a radiation; write 'the sequence of forms', never 'great-great-grandfather'; (b) the Basilosaurus hind limbs are about 35 cm on a 16 m animal and were almost certainly non-locomotory, most likely mating claspers — teach the real reading, not 'useless leftover legs', or the ladder contradicts its own sister ladder on vestigiality; (c) verify Gingerich's 1983 Pakicetus description date before keying a year on it. DINNER-TEST PAYOFF: T7 — DNA and a single ankle bone, two completely independent methods that could have contradicted each other, forced to the same answer, with the fossil experts turning out to be the ones who were wrong. DISTRACTOR MINE: the real rival hypothesis (mesonychids), real candidate living relatives (hippopotamus, pig, deer, camel), and the real historical misidentifications (sea serpent, giant marine reptile, Zeuglodon). LANE BORDER: the ANIMAL bank owns living whales — baleen feeding, song, dive physiology, blue-whale size; nothing alive is a wonder in this ladder, only the rocks and the evidence.
history_overlap: animal bank whale ladders (baleen, whale song, deep-diving physiology, blue-whale superlatives) — no living-whale marvels may appear here; geography bank may own Wadi Al-Hitan as an Egyptian World Heritage place — this ladder uses it as a fossil bed only; the vestigial ladder in this same sub-strand also touches whale pelvic bones — key them THERE as the definition and HERE as the fossil sequence.

name: Vestigial: what the body kept after the job ended
scope: CONCEPT ladder that fixes the most commonly mistaught idea in biology — and comes out with stronger evidence than the sloppy version had. T1: goosebumps are a fur response you still own — tiny arrector pili muscles yank each hair upright to trap warm air and make an animal look bigger; you kept the muscles and the wiring, on skin that no longer has the coat. T2: a human embryo grows a tail — clearly visible around week five or six, and at that stage longer than the leg buds — which is then normally reabsorbed, leaving the fused coccyx. T3: the correction most people need, and the ladder's spine — vestigial means a structure has lost its ANCESTRAL function, not that it does nothing. The coccyx anchors pelvic muscles and ligaments; whale pelvic bones anchor reproductive muscles; python spurs are used in mating. All three are still vestigial, because none of them is a tail or a leg any more. T4: the list shrinks when you look properly. In 1893 the anatomist Robert Wiedersheim catalogued a long roster of vestigial human structures; almost all of them turned out to have jobs, and honest biology quietly ate its own bad examples — including the spleen, dismissed as vestigial into the 1950s and now known to filter blood and mount immune responses. T5: the appendix is the case in point. Darwin took it for the shrunken remnant of a cecum used to digest leaves. In 2007 Randal Bollinger and William Parker argued it is a 'safe house' — a biofilm reservoir that reseeds the gut after everything is flushed out — and a 2012 study found that people without an appendix were about twice as likely to suffer recurrent Clostridioides difficile colitis. T6: the strongest evidence against 'useless leftover' comes from a family tree — Heather Smith's group estimated the appendix has evolved independently something like thirty-plus times across mammals and been lost only a handful of times. Nobody re-evolves a useless organ thirty times. T7: leftovers you can check on yourself right now — the plica semilunaris in the inner corner of your eye, the remnant of a third eyelid that a bird or a cat still sweeps across; the muscles that let a minority of people wiggle their ears; Darwin's tubercle on the rim of some ears; and the palmaris longus tendon, which a sizeable fraction of people simply do not have. T8: the cleanest cases are not human — blind cave fish that still start growing eyes as embryos and then lose them, and flightless birds carrying reduced wing bones and a shrunken keel.
source: Grokipedia, 'Vestigiality' (the three identifying criteria — extreme reduction relative to sister taxa, loss of specialized ancestral morphology, loss of the salient ancestral function; whale pelvic remnants and boa/python spurs; goosebumps as behavioural vestigiality; Darwin, Origin ch.13 on rudimentary and aborted organs; Aristotle on blind moles; Lamarck 1809 coining 'rudiment'/'vestige'; Wiedersheim's 1893 catalogue and its subsequent shrinkage; the spleen dismissed as vestigial until the late 1950s; appendix lymphoid tissue and microbiota reservoir); Wikipedia, 'Appendix (anatomy)' (Darwin's leaf-digesting-cecum account; Bollinger and Parker 2007 'safe house' hypothesis; the 2012 finding of roughly doubled C. difficile recurrence after appendectomy; Heather Smith et al. 2013 estimate of 32–38 independent origins with no more than six losses; 2016 correlation of appendix presence with cecal lymphoid tissue).
framing_note: A CORRECTED-MISCONCEPTION concept ladder whose wonder is that the HONEST definition is better evidence than the sloppy one. T1 keys something the kid can test on a cold morning. ACCURACY RAILS: (a) NEVER let any rung call a vestigial structure 'useless' — dismantling that word is the ladder's entire job; (b) Wiedersheim's count is quoted variously (commonly ~86 in one edition and ~180 in another) — verify before a number is used, or key the rung on the SHRINKING of the list rather than its size; (c) the appendix rung must credit Bollinger and Parker (2007) and state the C. difficile result as an association from one study, not as proof. VISION_MANDATED TRUE: this is the one topic in the sub-strand where a careless rung imports false balance. The bank's framing lists evolution as settled and celebrated, so the audit must confirm the ladder does NOT echo the non-sequitur that finding one function refutes vestigiality (some reference material on this topic carries exactly that argument and it must not leak into a rung), and equally does NOT sermonize at anyone. The rungs teach the definition and the evidence and stop. DINNER-TEST PAYOFF: T6 — an organ re-invented thirty-odd times independently is the opposite of a leftover, and it makes the evolutionary reading sharper, not weaker. DISTRACTOR MINE: the classic 'vestigial' claims that turned out wrong — tonsils, spleen, thymus, the coccyx-as-useless — plus real anatomical neighbours (cecum, ileum, gallbladder).
history_overlap: animal bank owns python spurs, cave fish and flightless birds as creature marvels — they may appear here only as one-line evidence, never as portraits; the walking-whales ladder in this same sub-strand also touches whale pelvic bones — that ladder keys the fossil sequence, this one keys the definition; any human-anatomy ladder in the physiology sub-strand owns the appendix as an organ that gets removed.

name: DNA: the evidence Darwin never had
scope: CONCEPT ladder — independent lines of evidence that could have contradicted each other and did not. T1: the same code runs everything alive. In 1978 a human insulin gene was put into bacteria and the bacteria made real human insulin; by 1982 diabetics were injecting it. A bacterium can read a human gene because the codebook is shared. T2: you carry a broken gene for vitamin C. That is why sailors got scurvy and dogs do not — the gene for the last enzyme in the pathway, GULO, is still sitting in your genome, disabled. Chimpanzees, gorillas, orangutans and monkeys of the same suborder carry the same disabled gene, inherited from one failure about 63 million years ago. T3: and it broke more than once, independently — guinea pigs lost theirs roughly 20 million years ago, at different places in the gene; some bats and some birds lost theirs separately again. Same handicap, different scars. That pattern is what descent predicts and coincidence does not. T4: a prediction about a chromosome nobody had looked at — humans have 23 pairs; chimpanzees, gorillas and orangutans all have 24. If we share ancestry, two of theirs must have fused into one of ours, and the join should still be visible. T5: it is. Human chromosome 2 carries telomere repeats — the caps that belong on the ENDS of chromosomes — stranded in the middle at band 2q13, pointing head to head, plus the remains of a second, dead centromere. Yunis and Prakash matched the banding in 1982; IJdo's team found the fusion sequence itself in 1991. T6: roughly a twelfth of your genome is old virus — endogenous retroviruses that inserted themselves into germ cells and were inherited ever after; many sit at the SAME position in the human and the chimpanzee genome, which makes sense only if one shared ancestor was infected once. T7: the molecular tree matched the bone tree. Cytochrome c, a protein in every breathing thing, differs between species by amounts that line up with the branching order paleontologists had already built from fossils, decades before anyone could read a protein. T8: an honest caveat — molecular clocks are not stopwatches. Rates vary between lineages and every calibration leans on a fossil, so molecular DATES carry real error bars; the branching ORDER is far more secure than the numbers attached to it. T9: Darwin published in 1859 with none of this, and missing the one thing he most needed — a mechanism of heredity. His own guess, pangenesis, was wrong; the right answer went into print in 1866 and nobody connected the two for a generation. T10: the ruins of a sense — humans carry hundreds of broken olfactory-receptor genes, a smell system in disrepair that a mouse still runs at full power.
source: Wikipedia, 'L-gulonolactone oxidase' (loss of GULO activity in Haplorhini about 63 million years ago at the haplorhine/strepsirrhine split; independent loss in guinea pigs about 20 million years ago; variable loss in bats, passerine birds and teleosts; Nishikimi et al. 1994 cloning and mapping of the human nonfunctional gene); Wikipedia, 'Chromosome 2' (23 vs 24 pairs in humans and other hominids; chimpanzee sequences split across two chromosomes; vestigial second centromere at q21.3–q22.1; interstitial telomeric sequences at 2q13; Yunis and Prakash 1982 banding; IJdo et al. 1991 fusion signature); Ohta & Nishikimi on shared GULO lesions in primates flagged for verification; ERV genome-fraction and human olfactory-pseudogene counts flagged for verification against current genome literature.
framing_note: The theme ladder that carries this sub-strand's T4/T5 analytic ceiling — the wonder is CONVERGENCE of independent methods, not any one fact. ACCURACY RAILS: (a) on GULO be exact — the claim is that haplorhine primates share ONE inherited break while guinea pigs and bats broke theirs SEPARATELY at different sites; do NOT assert 'identical mutations' without checking Ohta & Nishikimi, and if that check fails, key the rung on the shared 63-million-year-old inactivation versus the separate 20-million-year-old one; (b) the ERV genome fraction and the olfactory-pseudogene count both need verifying against current genome papers before authoring — seed, don't guess; (c) teach 'pseudogene', 'telomere' and 'centromere' before any rung tests them. DINNER-TEST PAYOFF: T4/T5 — a prediction made about a chromosome before anyone had looked, and the fusion scar sitting exactly where it had to be. DISTRACTOR MINE: real adjacent genetics that a thoughtful person would have to rule out — convergent evolution, horizontal gene transfer, gene duplication, mitochondrial inheritance — plus the real historical wrong answers (blending inheritance, Darwin's pangenesis, and protein-as-the-hereditary-molecule before Avery's 1944 result). ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let a stem say 'two chromosomes fused' and then ask what was found in the middle of chromosome 2 — state the COUNT MISMATCH (23 versus 24) as the puzzle and let the telomere scar be recalled.
history_overlap: science's own DNA sub-strand owns Watson, Crick, Franklin and Photo 51, the double helix and the cracking of the genetic code — this ladder must NOT retell the structure; it owns comparative genomics purely as EVIDENCE for common descent. Any Mendel ladder in the heredity sub-strand owns the peas — the T9 rung here is only Darwin's missing piece. The Wallace/Origin ladder in this same sub-strand also names pangenesis — keep it there as biography and here as the gap DNA filled.

name: The peppered moth, re-tested
scope: The textbook case that was attacked, and the only reply that counts. T1: in 1848 a collector named R. S. Edleston caught a black peppered moth near Manchester — the first anyone recorded. By 1895 roughly 98% of the peppered moths caught around Manchester were black. T2: the cause was industrial and unmysterious — coal soot blackened the bark, and sulphur dioxide killed the pale lichens that the speckled form matched. T3: in the 1950s Bernard Kettlewell tested the bird-predation explanation head-on: mark, release and recapture in polluted Birmingham woods and in unpolluted Dorset, and the survival advantage flipped depending on which wood you were standing in. T4: then it was attacked. Critics raised real methodological problems — moths released in daylight, and placed on tree TRUNKS when the species mostly rests higher up on branches — and a 2002 popular book pushed those criticisms into an accusation of fraud. The most famous demonstration of natural selection in a textbook suddenly looked shaky. T5: the answer was not an argument. It was a re-run. Michael Majerus spent seven years, from 2001 to 2007, releasing thousands of moths onto natural resting positions and watching birds take them himself. He died before he could publish; colleagues published the result in 2012, and differential bird predation was confirmed. T6: the Clean Air Act of 1956 then ran the experiment backwards. As the soot cleared, the black form fell from over 90% to under 5% at surveyed sites — selection reversing when the environment reversed, watched in real time. T7: the mechanism was finally pinned in 2016: the melanic form comes from a transposable element — a piece of jumping DNA — that inserted itself into cortex, a wing-patterning gene; the insertion was dated to around 1819, a generation before Edleston's moth. T8: the mathematics arrived first. J. B. S. Haldane calculated in 1924 that a selection pressure of the size involved could take a dominant variant from rarity to near-fixation in roughly fifty generations — and the collectors' records show almost exactly that.
source: Grokipedia, 'Peppered moth evolution' (Edleston's 1848 Manchester specimen reported 1864; ~98% melanic in Manchester by 1895; soot deposition and SO2-driven lichen loss; Kettlewell's 1950s mark-release-recapture in Birmingham and Dorset with roughly 2:1 survival advantage reversing by site; the real criticisms — artificial positioning on trunks contrary to natural branch/canopy resting, lichen staining; Majerus's 1990s–2000s targeted observations vindicating avian selection; Clean Air Act 1956 and 1968 amendments, melanic frequency falling from >90% to under 5%; carbonaria as a single dominant autosomal allele; the transposable-element insertion in the cortex gene; Haldane's 1924 calculation of selection coefficient ~0.3 and ~50 generations to near-fixation); van't Hof et al. 2016 (Nature) flagged for verification of the ~1819 insertion date; Cook, Grant, Saccheri & Mallet 2012 flagged for verification of Majerus's release numbers and the posthumous publication.
framing_note: The sub-strand's METHOD flagship: what you actually DO when a famous result is challenged. T1 inverts the wonder — the 98% figure is the hook and the creature is the answer. ACCURACY RAILS: (a) the 2002 fraud accusation (Judith Hooper, Of Moths and Men) was NOT sustained; the methodological criticisms were legitimate and the fraud charge was rejected by the researchers who checked it. The rung must key what was CHECKABLE and must never leave a child believing a scientist was caught cheating; (b) verify Majerus's numbers — years, moths released, the 2012 authorship — before authoring; (c) verify the ~1819 date for the cortex insertion. DINNER-TEST PAYOFF: T5 — a man answered a public accusation by spending seven years redoing the experiment properly in his own garden, and died before the result appeared. DISTRACTOR MINE: the rival explanations serious biologists genuinely proposed for industrial melanism — thermoregulation (dark wings absorb heat faster), direct induction by pollutants, migration from other populations, heterozygote advantage — plus real adjacent biologists (Haldane, E. B. Ford, Kettlewell, Majerus). LANE: the moth is a VEHICLE for the method; do not let any rung become an animal portrait — no life-cycle, no caterpillar-twig-mimicry rung, that is the animal bank's.
history_overlap: history and geography banks may own the Industrial Revolution and Manchester's soot as an era-and-place story — this ladder uses the soot only as the selective pressure and the Clean Air Act only as its removal; animal bank owns the peppered moth caterpillar's twig mimicry as a creature adaptation.

name: Lamarck's ghost: what a body can and cannot pass on
scope: MINI ladder whose job is to make the bank's richest distractor honest. T1: the story everyone remembers — giraffes stretching for high leaves and handing longer necks to their calves — is Jean-Baptiste Lamarck's, published in 1809, and it is the most repeated wrong answer in biology; the same book also gave us the useful word 'vestige' for a reduced organ. T2: it was tested about as bluntly as a thing can be tested. August Weismann cut the tails off 68 white mice through five generations — 901 offspring, and not one born with a shortened tail — and argued that body cells simply cannot write back to the cells that make the next generation. T3: the honest modern twist. Children conceived during the Dutch Hunger Winter of 1944–45 showed measurable health differences decades later, and in 2008 researchers found altered chemical methylation marks at the IGF2 gene in that same cohort — the famine left an annotation on the DNA. T4: say exactly what that IS and IS NOT. Methylation marks sit ON the DNA; they do not rewrite the sequence. Most are stripped between generations. Whether such marks are reliably passed down across generations in mammals is genuinely unsettled, and the bank says so plainly: no one yet knows. Lamarck is not back. Something smaller and stranger is on the table.
source: Wikipedia, 'August Weismann' (68 white mice over five generations, 901 young with not a single rudimentary tail, published in Essays upon Heredity, 1889; germ plasm theory and the soma-to-germline barrier; Weismann's own acknowledgement that the test addressed mutilation-inheritance specifically and could not rule out every Lamarckian claim); Grokipedia, 'Vestigiality' (Lamarck, Philosophie Zoologique 1809, coining 'rudiment' and 'vestige' and citing the reduced eyes of burrowing spalax moles under use-and-disuse); Heijmans et al. 2008 (PNAS) on periconceptional-famine-associated IGF2 methylation in the Dutch Hunger Winter cohort — flagged for verification of cohort details and effect size.
framing_note: A MYSTERY-mode mini ladder. Its purpose is that a child who meets 'Lamarck' as a wrong answer in ten other rungs should know WHY he was wrong and, equally, why 'epigenetics proves Lamarck right' is a bad take. ACCURACY RAILS: (a) Weismann's own caveat matters — he said himself that the experiment settled mutilation-inheritance, not every Lamarckian claim; do not overstate it into a knockout of everything Lamarck proposed; (b) on transgenerational epigenetic inheritance in humans the bank says PLAINLY that this is open — and per the MYSTERY rule, no distractor may secretly be the truth, and no rung may imply that acquired traits are inherited; (c) verify the Heijmans 2008 IGF2 finding and the Dutch Hunger Winter cohort details before authoring. DINNER-TEST PAYOFF: T2 — 901 mice, five generations of cut tails, every single pup born with a tail. DISTRACTOR MINE: the real graveyard of heredity theories — use and disuse, pangenesis, orthogenesis, blending inheritance, and Lysenko's vernalization, all of which serious people held. LANE BORDER: Lysenko and state-enforced Lamarckism belong to the bank's science-and-the-state ladder; this ladder may name Lysenkoism inside a distractor but must NOT take the Vavilov story.
history_overlap: science's own Lysenko / censorship-of-dissent ladder in the howscience section owns Vavilov, the imprisoned Soviet geneticists and state-enforced biology — do not take any of it here; any Mendel or heredity ladder owns the actual mechanism of inheritance; history bank may own the Dutch Hunger Winter as a WWII episode — this ladder uses only the cohort's biological finding.
